pr_title: Allow bigger json parsing to JsonDocument
pr_body:
Big json would cause internal metadata array length to overflow, thus throwing an exception.

After this change, this case is handled similar to List\<T\>.Grow allowing array to expand to it's possible maximum.

I don't think it is reasonable to include a test for this case, because it uses too much memory.

Closes #70785

@eiriktsarpalis My local test is the reproduction in the issue and it uses almost 3.5gb of RAM, if this is fine then I can include it. I don't think it's possible to test it any other way.

Generally it's fine to add tests that use lots of memory, but we generally force them to run serially, potentially make them outer loop, and sometimes just make them manual (disabled by default and only run by developers touching relevant code). You should assume that automation will run tests on devices that are slow and don't have much memory, and other tests by default will run concurrently.

Looking at our current [test coverage of OOM exceptions](https://grep.app/search?q=Assert.Throws%3COutOfMemoryException%3E&filter[repo][0]=dotnet/runtime), we only seem to do this for cases where large size can be predetermined by arguments and never involve actually creating an ~ `Array.MaxLength` sized buffer. So it seems like not testing is fine.

@Paul-Grimes could you confirm that @svick's reproduction matches your own stacktrace?

I suspect that the particular error occurs because of an arithmetic overflow in JsonDocument's Enlarge method:
https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/3fc61ebb562afc327a8fc6de5c82d76e86bf6f5d/src/libraries/System.Text.Json/src/System/Text/Json/Document/JsonDocument.MetadataDb.cs#L234

The enlarge method could be improved to better handle boundary conditions, e.g. taking inspiration from List<T>'s internal `Grow` function:
https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/3fc61ebb562afc327a8fc6de5c82d76e86bf6f5d/src/libraries/System.Private.CoreLib/src/System/Collections/Generic/List.cs#L425-L429

Fundamentally though, this is hitting the limits of JsonDocument design, I don't believe the type is capable of handling arbitrarily large JSON data.

@eiriktsarpalis this is the my full exception:

```
System.ArgumentOutOfRangeException
  HResult=0x80131502
  Message=Specified argument was out of the range of valid values. (Parameter 'minimumLength')
  Source=System.Private.CoreLib
  StackTrace:
   at System.Buffers.TlsOverPerCoreLockedStacksArrayPool`1.Rent(Int32 minimumLength)
   at System.Text.Json.JsonDocument.MetadataDb.Enlarge()
   at System.Text.Json.JsonDocument.Parse(ReadOnlySpan`1 utf8JsonSpan, JsonReaderOptions readerOptions, MetadataDb& database, StackRowStack& stack)
   at System.Text.Json.JsonDocument.ParseUnrented(ReadOnlyMemory`1 utf8Json, JsonReaderOptions readerOptions, JsonTokenType tokenType)
   at System.Text.Json.JsonDocument.ParseValue(ReadOnlyMemory`1 json, JsonDocumentOptions options)
   at System.Text.Json.Nodes.JsonNode.Parse(String json, Nullable`1 nodeOptions, JsonDocumentOptions documentOptions)
   at Program.<Main>$(String[] args) in C:\Code\ProviderIdentifcationChallenge\ProviderIdentifcationChallenge\Program.cs:line 19
```
I looks the same as @svick's

@Paul-Grimes In the meantime, I would recommend using one of streaming deserialization methods for large JSON data, e.g. `JsonSerializer.DeserializeAsync` or `DeserializeAsyncEnumerable` for long root-level arrays.

review_comments: Shouldn't this also verify that `toReturn.Length` is less than the max length?
Should it throw an `OutOfMemoryException` if they're equal? With message like "Data capacity exceeded supported range"

Here's how List<T> does it:

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/202ccdb59afedcf2d7e86b3ba10a2b9a703c71c9/src/libraries/System.Private.CoreLib/src/System/Collections/Generic/List.cs#L461-L463

Seems like a good approach to copy.
That's about right. But rather than throwing an exception explicitly you could try setting `newCapacity` to `int.MaxValue` or something so that the buffer pool throws the right exception for you.
